newsitem.title: TURKEY: Turk parliament drops first charge against Ciller.
newsitem.headline: Turk parliament drops first charge against Ciller.

text.p: The Turkish parliament dropped the first of two corruption charges that Deputy Prime Minister Tansu Ciller faced on Tuesday, in balloting seen as a test of the Islamist-led coalition's unity.
MPs voted 327 to 172 not to send Ciller, also the foreign minister, to the Supreme Court on accusations that she failed to prevent corruption at the TEDAS electricity company.

"The commission report on former prime minister Tansu Ciller has been accepted," deputy speaker Kemer Genc said. A parliament probe had recommended dropping the charges against Ciller, Turkey's first woman leader. She was prime minister from 1993-96.
MPs were to vote later on Tuesday on whether to send her to the Supreme Court on the more serious charge of illegally interfering with the sale of state-owned carmaker TOFAS.
Prime Minister Necmettin Erbakan's Islamist-led government would be in deep trouble if coalition partner Ciller lost either of the votes.
The administration is at one of its lowest points since its formation last June. Erbakan was confident his government would be strengthened by the votes.
"The things they are doing, censure motions and the rest of it, are useful. They will show just how well everything is going," he told MPs of his Welfare Party earlier in the day.
Ciller faces a third corruption vote in parliament on Wednesday, on the source of her personal wealth,
The government must deal with an opposition censure motion next week that accuses it of threatening Turkey's secular system with plans to increase the role of Islam in public life.
Ministers in Ciller's True Path Party forced Erbakan to drop a proposals to scrap a ban on female civil servants wearing Islamic headscarves in the workplace.
The coalition is under pressure from a tide of street demonstrations that started as protests at a security scandal but have turned into displays of general dissent.
The interior ministry has ordered provincial governors to take security measures against potential trouble at the nightly protests, Anatolian news agency said.
"As it is seems such protests will continue for a time...I request that all necessary security arrangements and measures be taken," it quoted Interior Minister Meral Aksener as saying.
Many Turks switch off their lights, sound car horns or take to the streets with lighted candles each night at nine p.m. for demonstrations dubbed "One minute's darkness for enlightenment."

The media has accused state officials of close links to organised crime and death squads after a gangster and a senior policeman died in the same car in a crash last November. A government MP was a passenger.
